The CSV values are the ones quoted here; the point estimates agree.

Report section 8 names R4 (TACO) and R2 (ARCTIC) as the best temporal representation; saturation_summary.csv column best_temporal is R5 on both datasets (R4 is 0.5 % behind on TACO, R2 1.7 % behind on ARCTIC).
On ARCTIC the interval of R2's temporal gap to the best includes 0; on TACO it does not.
Same fixed-probe and fixed-recipe qualifiers as the other F2-A / F2-B entries.

entries.claim: By the report's pre-specified saturation rule against FULL, R2 is the smallest representation saturated on both the wrench axis and the future-structure axis on both datasets at the 2.5 % and 5 % thresholds; applied against the best representation of each axis, the same rule selects R3 or R5 instead (R2 only at 10 % on ARCTIC).
entries.metric: Saturation rule (plan.md 'Decisions'; aggregate.py::saturation): gap = error ratio to the reference - 1 for the wrench probe (functional) and for the T1-T4 composite (temporal); a representation is saturated on an axis when gap < threshold (0.025, 0.05 or 0.1) OR the lower end of the gap's bootstrap 95 % interval is <= 0; the choice is the smallest-dimensional representation saturated on both axes. Reference = FULL (the planned rule) or the lowest-error representation of the axis ('best').
caveats: Against FULL the rule is passed with NEGATIVE gaps: every representation from R2 upward is 'saturated' because FULL is worse under the fixed probe and recipe, not because the dense state was matched. The report therefore reports the rule against the best representation side by side; the page should show both readings.

'Sufficient' means sufficient for the modelled wrench proxy and for the structured targets T1-T4 under these fixed models; it is the report's operational term, not a proof of sufficiency or optimality.

On the temporal axis alone R1 (participation + amount, 12 numbers) already passes the rule against FULL on both datasets (TACO gap -0.0107, ARCTIC gap 0.0155 with an interval reaching below 0); R2 is selected because of the wrench axis.
The rule accepts a representation when its gap's interval contains zero, which is lenient at small n (ARCTIC, 44 test takes) - stated in report section 10.
The report labels the outcome 'Case A of the request with the persistence qualification'; the list of alternative cases is not stored with the report.

entries.claim: Under the fixed probe and the fixed temporal recipe the full dense state shows no structured advantage: replacing R5 by FULL roughly doubles the wrench-probe error (x 2.04 TACO, x 2.27 ARCTIC) and raises the composite future-structure error by 34 % (TACO) and 67 % (ARCTIC); in these two experiments the dense input is better only at predicting the dense future itself. The report reads this as a statement about the parameterisation and the fixed models, not about information; at event level on TACO the dense change is the better tracker of the retention-based wrench change.

entries.correction_reason: Numbers confirmed (incremental_gain.csv). Two fixes. (1) R5 -> FULL is not 'adding' anything: FULL = contact map + hand points and holds none of R5's blocks; the table merely labels the step 'dense detail'. (2) 'Better only at predicting the dense future' is too broad once Experiment C is counted: event_correlations.csv, TACO all persistent events, Spearman with 1 - retention is 0.421 [0.360, 0.485] for the dense change vs 0.214 [0.129, 0.295] for the R2 change (persistent spatial 0.274 vs 0.110; ARCTIC persistent spatial 0.595 vs 0.352), and on TACO the dense change misses fewer large wrench changes (event_quadrants.csv frac_large_w_missed 0.232-0.268 vs 0.339 for d_R2). The page phrase 'dense contact is over-specified' is not a measured property.

entries.claim: Measured by the paired per-frame error ratios, the model fed the R2 window does not beat carrying the current target forward at a one-frame horizon on either dataset; at eight frames its error is below persistence on TACO for participation, amount, normal and wrench profile but not for the centroid, and on ARCTIC it is above persistence for every target at every horizon. For participation the ranking metric disagrees: by macro AUPRC the same model is above the persistence line at every horizon on both datasets.

caveats: This caveat must stay attached to any 'R2 preserves future structured contact evolution' sentence: the evidence is the ranking of inputs under one recipe, not an absolute forecasting result. The report explains the level by the recipe (absolute targets, input noise, projection, early stopping; no model receives the current target explicitly) - section 5 'Persistence' and section 10.

By macro AUPRC (a ranking metric) the R2 model is above persistence for participation on ARCTIC at h = 8 (0.9286 vs 0.8383 in temporal_prediction.csv), while the per-frame probability error used in the composite is 1.47 times persistence's; the two measures disagree and the page should not cite only the favourable one.

Code reading, not in the report: for centroid and normal the persistence error is averaged over parts active at both t and t + h, the model error over parts active at t + h (train_temporal.py lines 149-153; n_frames 18069 vs 19353 on TACO), so the centroid ratio is not like for like.

entries.claim_as_extracted: In absolute terms the model fed the R2 window does not beat carrying the current target forward at a one-frame horizon on either dataset; at eight frames it beats persistence on TACO for participation, amount, normal and wrench profile but not for the centroid, and on ARCTIC it is worse than persistence for every target at every horizon.
entries.correction_reason: All 20 ratios confirmed in temporal_ratios.csv (vs = PERSIST), ARCTIC intervals exclude 1 at h = 1, 4, 8. But the participation ratio is the per-frame |p - a| error; temporal_prediction.csv gives macro AUPRC R2 0.997 / 0.984 / 0.974 vs persistence 0.978 / 0.930 / 0.899 (TACO) and 0.995 / 0.968 / 0.929 vs 0.970 / 0.899 / 0.838 (ARCTIC), and the report's own prose says the models beat persistence on ARCTIC 'only for participation'. Without the metric qualifier the sentence contradicts the report. The centroid / normal ratios are not like for like (model: parts active at t + h; persistence: parts active at both frames; train_temporal.py lines 149-153).

The residual is what THIS frame-wise MLP decoder leaves, 'not a canonical decomposition' (report section 10). The decoder sees only the 48 numbers of R2 (no object descriptor) and all three R2 decoders ran to the 60-epoch cap on both datasets (logs/residual_*_R2_seed*.log), so the residual share is an upper bound on what R2 leaves undetermined.
Wording: the residual is a realization residual / within-structure variation, never 'noise' - the report's Q6 heading is 'persistent variation, not structure and not noise'.

No page-ready qualitative image exists for 'same structure, different dense realization'. The six figures/figG_examples_*.png are four-row diagnostic sheets (1870 x 1540 px, 7-pt table, internal labels such as d_Cfull). The closest candidate, reports/structure_variance_boundary/figures/figG_examples_taco_variation_733_1.png (513106 bytes), would be usable only cropped to its top two rows (pre / post contact views, roughly y = 45-890 px) with a new caption: one TACO event in which the same five fingers stay on a plate with similar amounts while the contacts slide; dense change 5.07 (train median 1.05), R2 change 0.44 (median 0.66), wrench-profile change 0.13 (median 0.20), retention 0.77 (figures/figG_examples.csv). It is the LARGEST dense change among 52 candidates (figures.py::fig_g), and its R2 change is below the median, not zero - 'similar coarse structure', not 'same structure'.

entries.correction_reason: All ratios confirmed for Z* = R2. Rewording needed for scope and verb: (a) 'follows the future structure' reads as a mechanism; the measurement is that the oracle with the future R2 lowers the error (0.69 / 0.43 / 0.38 TACO, 0.81 / 0.76 / 0.80 ARCTIC). (b) The ARCTIC null is specific to the R2 residual: for the residual left by R3 the same causal predictor reads 1.000 / 0.972 / 0.925 with the h = 8 interval [0.880, 0.974] excluding 1. (c) The learned ratios are 3-seed means over a seed-0 baseline, an offset of about 1-2 % - the size of the ARCTIC effects. Never 'noise', never null-space (report section 10).

dataset_differences: Scope: this study covers TACO and ARCTIC only. OakInk2 was excluded (report section 8: its cached event sequences carry no hand geometry in the object frame); nothing in F2-A / F2-B / F2-C / F2-subA / F2-subB may be extended to OakInk2.

Statistical weight: TACO has 186 test takes (22245 probe frames), ARCTIC 44 (10567); ARCTIC intervals are 2-3 times wider and the saturation rule (which accepts a gap whose interval reaches 0) is more lenient there.

Size of the R2 step on the wrench probe: R1 -> R2 multiplies the error by 0.51 on TACO and by 0.36 on ARCTIC; participation alone leaves a larger wrench error on ARCTIC (R0 0.507 vs 0.367). The amount block (R0 -> R1) helps the wrench on TACO (0.943 [0.932, 0.952]) and not on ARCTIC (1.005 [0.998, 1.012]).
Best representation on the wrench axis: R5 on TACO, R3 on ARCTIC; R2 is 13.4 % above the best on TACO and 7.6 % on ARCTIC.
R2 versus FULL on the future-structure composite: 18 % lower on TACO, 32 % lower on ARCTIC; the dense detail (R5 -> FULL) costs x 1.34 on TACO and x 1.67 on ARCTIC (wrench probe x 2.04 and x 2.27).

R2's temporal gap to the best: 4.0 % [3.1, 5.0] on TACO (interval excludes 0) versus 1.7 % [-0.6, 3.9] on ARCTIC (interval includes 0). Consequently the rule against the best picks R5 (2.5 %) / R3 (5 %, 10 %) on TACO and R3 (2.5 %, 5 %) / R2 (10 %) on ARCTIC; against FULL at the 10 % threshold it picks R1 on TACO and R2 on ARCTIC.

Coarse hand (F2-subA): lowers the horizon-averaged future-structure composite by 2.2 % on TACO (5.1 % at h = 8) and not on ARCTIC (1.012 [0.993, 1.035]); R3 -> R5 gives a small wrench gain on TACO only (0.985 [0.970, 0.997]).
Topology (F2-subB): wrench error -10.4 % on TACO, -7.0 % on ARCTIC; temporal composite -0.8 % on TACO (interval excludes 1), unchanged on ARCTIC.

Persistence: the R2-input model beats persistence at h = 8 on TACO for participation, amount, normal and wrench profile (ratios 0.91-0.94) but on ARCTIC it is worse than persistence for every target at every horizon (1.10-1.68 at h = 8).
Residual share left by R2 (1 - decoder R2): 10.7 % (contact map) / 15.2 % (hand points) on TACO versus 25.6 % / 30.8 % on ARCTIC - ARCTIC's dense state is less determined by the coarse state.
Residual persistence: the last value leaves 19 % / 50 % / 75 % of the contact residual's energy at h = 1 / 4 / 8 on TACO versus 9 % / 26 % / 42 % on ARCTIC (more persistent on ARCTIC).

Residual change: on TACO the causal change predictor removes 4 % / 14 % / 20 % of the last-value error (intervals exclude 1); on ARCTIC 0 % / 0 % / 2 % (intervals include 1). Hand-point residual: oracle removes 31 / 57 / 62 % on TACO versus 19 / 24 / 20 % on ARCTIC; causal 22 / 36 / 46 % versus 11 / 4 / 0 %.

Event level: the share of large dense changes with small R2 and small wrench change is 24 % [15, 34] on TACO (n = 75) and 18 % [0, 50] on ARCTIC (n = 11); a finger exchange changes the wrench profile about 2.6 times as much as sliding on ARCTIC (0.266 vs 0.100) but only about 1.2 times on TACO (0.164 vs 0.136).
do_not_claim: That R2 is the optimal, minimal or necessary representation: the ladder is one path through the space of descriptors, R2 is not the lowest-error rung on either axis, and the rule against FULL is passed because FULL is worse under the fixed models.

That the dense contact map contains less information than R2, or that dense detail is irrelevant: R2 is computed from the dense state; the report calls the dense inputs' higher error 'a statement about the parameterisation, not about the information'. 'Over-specified' is page wording, not a measured property.

That R2 predicts the future contact well in absolute terms: the R2-input model is worse than persistence at h = 1 on both datasets and at every horizon on ARCTIC; only the ranking of inputs under one fixed recipe is evidence.
That R2 is sufficient for predicting the dense future contact: from an R2 window the future dense contact map is predicted 1.3-2.3 times worse than from FULL.

That R2 preserves human intent, real grasp stability or physical feasibility: the functional target is a modelled, normalised wrench capability (unit finger budgets, mu = 0.5, one hand) - a proxy for functional grasp capability.

That R2 is only a wrench descriptor, or conversely that its temporal role is established independently of the wrench: one of the four composite targets (T4) is the future wrench profile, and on the temporal axis alone R1 already passes the rule against FULL.
That the residual is noise, random, or (biological / robot) null-space motion: it is persistent, the report says 'not structure and not noise', and no Jacobian null space was measured.

That the residual is unpredictable without qualification: on TACO the causal predictor removes 4 / 14 / 20 % of the last-value error, the hand-point residual partly follows the future structure on both datasets, and 'not predictable' means 'not by these models from this context'.

That '11-15 %' or '26-31 %' are confidence intervals or ranges over runs: the two ends are the contact-map block and the hand-point block; the values are 1 - R2 of one frame-wise decoder (an upper bound, decoder trained to the epoch cap, no object descriptor as input).

That the coarse hand pose is useless or 'adds <= 2 %' everywhere: it lowers the TACO composite by 5 % at h = 8, it helps predict the future hand (x 0.64 / x 0.58) and it lowers the strict-profile error in the one-seed sensitivity.
That topology does not matter: it lowers the wrench-probe error by 10 % (TACO) / 7 % (ARCTIC) and is what the rule selects when the wrench must match the best representation closely.

That all spatial changes are functionally irrelevant or that sliding does not change the wrench: sliding events still change the wrench profile by a median 0.10-0.14, and only 24 % (TACO) / 18 % (ARCTIC) of large dense changes fall in the small-R2-change and small-wrench-change quadrant.
A pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any statement about OakInk2, for these blocks.

That this study shows a generator should be built on R2 or that R2 supervision helps generation: it is a diagnostic with small probes and fixed predictors - no generative model and no rollout were run here.

The report's prose interval '4.0 % [2.7, 5.2]' / '1.7 % [-1.8, 5.1]' for R2's temporal gap to the best, or its section-8 statement that the best temporal representation is R4 (TACO) / R2 (ARCTIC): the tables give [3.1, 5.0] / [-0.6, 3.9] and R5 on both.
That 'finger exchanges change the wrench twice as much as sliding' on both datasets: it holds on ARCTIC only.

That the figG example sheets show 'the same structure with a different dense realization': the 'variation' examples are the largest dense change among events whose R2 change is below the train median (not zero), and the ARCTIC one has a large amount change.

Caveat to attach to F2-B ('full dense contact provides no structured advantage'): the event-level analysis is not uniformly in favour of R2. event_correlations.csv, Spearman with 1 - retention: TACO all persistent events 0.421 [0.360, 0.485] (dense change) vs 0.214 [0.129, 0.295] (R2 change), TACO persistent spatial 0.274 vs 0.110, ARCTIC persistent spatial 0.595 vs 0.352; with the wrench-profile change d_q the order is the other way on persistent spatial events (TACO 0.371 vs 0.320, ARCTIC 0.624 vs 0.400). On TACO the dense change also misses fewer large wrench changes (event_quadrants.csv frac_large_w_missed 0.232 for d_FULL, 0.268 for d_CONTACT_FULL, 0.339 for d_R2; ARCTIC 0.400 vs 0.267 the other way). The extractor's entries quote none of this.

Caveat to attach to every 'worse than persistence' statement: the participation comparison depends on the metric. Per-frame |p - a| error: R2 model above persistence (ratios in temporal_ratios.csv). Macro AUPRC: R2 model above the persistence line at every horizon on both datasets (temporal_prediction.csv), and the report prose says 'on ARCTIC only for participation' the models beat persistence. The extractor's caveat mentions only ARCTIC h = 8.

Training-regime caveat as worded by the extractor is imprecise: the logs give the best-validation step (400-2600; 55 of 96 runs at 400-600) and a stop by patience 2000 steps later (2400-4600) out of a 30000-step budget; the report prose says 'best validation at 400-2 200 steps'. Say 'early-stopped, checkpoint taken at step 400-2600'.

The against-best reading of the saturation rule is not pre-specified: plan.md defines the rule against FULL only ('CI of the gap includes 0 or the gap < 2.5 / 5 / 10 %'); the best-representation reference was added in aggregate.py when FULL turned out not to be the best. The implemented test is 'lower bound <= 0', which also passes a representation that is significantly better than the reference. The page should call only the FULL rule 'pre-specified'.

The step R5 -> FULL (and the x axis R5 -> CONTACT_FULL -> FULL in the ladder figures) is a change of parameterisation, not an added block: FULL = dense contact map + 100 hand points and contains none of the compact blocks explicitly; R2 is itself computed from the dense state. Any 'adding the dense detail' sentence on the page needs this qualifier (now in the note of f2a_block_gain).

Baseline of the residual ratios: verified in aggregate.py that the residual energy and the last-value error come from the seed-0 decoder while the learned predictors are 3-seed means with their own decoders. My check of the per-frame NPZ files shows the three-seed mean last-value error is about 1-2 % above the seed-0 value on the contact block of both datasets; this is a checker's diagnostic, not a page number, but it means ARCTIC contact ratios of 1.03 / 1.02 / 0.975 cannot be read as 'worse' or 'better' than persistence. The figure notes now say so.

'Fixed probe' needs one qualifier the extractor did not attach: the architecture is fixed (2 hidden layers of width 256, plus the 1032-D object descriptor G), but dropout / weight decay are chosen on validation per representation from a 2 x 2 grid (probe_functional.py docstring; report section 4).

Page wording to avoid, not covered by a source: 'dense contact is over-specified for the meaningful temporal task' (the sources support only 'no structured advantage under the tested fixed probe and recipe', and the report calls the dense inputs' higher error 'a statement about the parameterisation, not about the information'); '<= 2 %' for the coarse hand (INDEX.md wording; the table gives 2.2 % averaged over horizons and 5.1 % at h = 8 on TACO); 'finger exchanges change the wrench twice as much as sliding' (ARCTIC only) and the extractor's derived '2.6 times' (the quotient of the two medians rounds to 2.7 and is in no source - quote the medians); 'participation alone halves the error' (TACO only).
